What Is a Stock Market Index and How Do ETFs Work?
5 min read
Beginner Guide
What Is a Stock Market Index and How Do ETFs Work?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: ETF ownership, fund-diversification limitations and the distinction between an index and a fund were compared with SEC Investor.gov fund guidance. Named index methodology and current holdings require dated issuer documents.

Compare different stock-index methodologies and learn how index-tracking ETFs provide specified exposure rather than ownership of an entire market.

What Is a Stock Market Index?

A stock index summarizes a selected set of securities using published rules. The S&P 500 measures a large-company segment using float-adjusted market-capitalization weighting, the Nasdaq Composite covers eligible Nasdaq-listed common-type securities, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index of 30 companies. The Nasdaq-100 is a distinct index covering a selected group of large non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies. These have different constituents and weighting methods; consult dated index methodology documents for current details.

An index is a calculation rather than a security purchased directly. Some exchange-traded funds seek to track named indexes using a specified portfolio and method. Fees, replication choices and distributions can cause a fund's return to differ from a reported index.

When a report states that 'the market' rose, identify its index, interval, currency and dividend treatment. A price index, total-return index and tracking ETF are distinct observations.

How ETFs Work

An ETF has shares that trade on an exchange and pursues an objective specified in its prospectus. Examples include SPY (S&P 500), QQQ (Nasdaq-100) and DIA (Dow Jones Industrial Average). An ETF shareholder owns shares of that fund rather than separately registered shares in every underlying company. Holdings, fees and returns may differ from those of its reference index.

An ETF provides the exposure specified by its objective and holdings. Diversification, concentration, leverage, annual expenses and trading costs vary by fund; low cost or broad diversification is not guaranteed. Read the current fund documents before interpreting a historical comparison.

Compare ETF examples with an individual company using the same period and position value in the simulator. Examine holdings and concentration rather than treating any fund as a universally appropriate beginner investment. Several funds can hold overlapping securities.

Building a Portfolio with ETFs

As a hypothetical accounting exercise, compare a 60% SPY, 20% QQQ and 20% cash allocation with another allocation that also totals 100%. These are arbitrary practice settings, not a suggested beginner portfolio. Overlapping holdings can create concentration even when several instruments are used.

Sector, regional and thematic ETFs offer differing exposure, but the name alone does not establish diversification, concentration or risk. Compare dated holdings, weights, fees and tracking objectives.

For a virtual portfolio comparison, hold constant the initial notional value and observation period for an ETF and a single-company example. Record overlapping holdings and missing distributions or execution costs. This study does not establish that the virtual allocation is truly diversified or that a real strategy would perform similarly.

How to Build a Balanced Virtual Portfolio from Scratch
6 min read
Beginner Guide
How to Build a Balanced Virtual Portfolio from Scratch

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source and arithmetic check: SEC Investor.gov diversification guidance and the hypothetical 25% × 30% × $100,000 = $7,500 sector-loss example were checked. No asset allocation or rebalancing schedule is recommended.

Learn the fundamentals of portfolio construction — asset allocation, diversification, and rebalancing — using your $100,000 TradeHQ virtual cash.

The Foundation: Asset Allocation

Asset allocation divides a portfolio across selected asset classes or holdings. Its effect depends on exposures, correlations and the period examined. Allocation does not guarantee diversification or performance; document the assumptions rather than rank it as universally more important than every other decision.

For a virtual accounting example, choose percentages that total 100%, such as 60% in a stock-index example, 30% cash and 10% another practice asset. These numbers illustrate weighting only. Compare another normalized allocation and identify overlapping holdings and concentration.

Real-money allocation depends on circumstances including objectives, time horizon, liabilities and ability to bear loss. Age alone cannot determine a suitable stock/bond split. A simulator can compare hypothetical exposures, but it cannot discover a person's true risk tolerance or certify an investment allocation.

Diversification: Don't Put All Eggs in One Basket

Diversification distributes selected exposures but cannot prevent several holdings declining together. For arithmetic practice, if a sector is 25% of a $100,000 virtual portfolio and falls 30% while everything else stays unchanged, that sector contributes a $7,500 loss before costs. Actual results depend on overlapping holdings and how other prices change.

Compare exposures by issuer, sector, geography, currency and economic sensitivity. More tickers do not necessarily mean less concentration when holdings overlap. An index fund provides a specified basket, not every type of protection.

Compare a concentrated virtual portfolio with one spread across different practice exposures. Keep total starting value and observation period equal and record each contribution to gains and losses. A commodity or ETF is not an assured hedge; correlations and fund holdings can change.

Rebalancing and Ongoing Management

Portfolio weights can drift as holdings change in value. In a hypothetical portfolio with no cash flows, a 50% crypto gain and a 10% stock gain increase crypto's relative weight. This changes sensitivity to crypto; the calculation alone does not determine the portfolio's overall risk. Rebalancing adjusts toward selected target weights through purchases, sales or new contributions where available. Targets are study assumptions, and fees, taxes and subsequent price changes affect the comparison. Rebalancing does not guarantee smaller losses or higher returns.

Rebalancing adjusts holdings toward selected target weights, subject to fills, rounding and costs. Timing and thresholds are choices to compare, not universal quarterly or five-percent rules. Rebalancing can add costs and can reduce returns in a continuing trend, so record turnover and compare against a portfolio left unchanged.

For an educational rebalancing worksheet, set hypothetical weights, recalculate them after invented price changes and quantify the effect of virtual transaction fees. Compare the adjusted portfolio with one left unchanged. No allocation, monthly schedule or calculated benefit should be treated as a recommendation for a real account.

Beginner Guide
Risk Management for Paper Trading: Risk Budgets and Exits

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited calculation and source check: 0.4×2−0.6×1=0.2, 0.25×3−0.75×1=0, and 192×(5+0.10+0.095)=997.44 were recalculated. SEC order guidance supports the limitations of stop orders. No strategy performance or suitability claim was verified.

Study position sizing, conceptual exits and risk-budget arithmetic. TradeHQ supports manual market orders; percentage rules such as 1% or 2% are worksheet assumptions.

Measuring Risk Alongside Trade Outcomes

Risk management describes how exposure and losses are measured or limited under a chosen process. Profitability also depends on realized gains, losses, frequency and costs. For example, a 40% win rate with fixed 2R gains and 1R losses has gross expectancy 0.4×2−0.6×1=0.2R per trade before costs; it is hypothetical arithmetic.

Exposure rules and intended exits can be compared in a hypothetical worksheet, but they do not guarantee survival through a loss sequence or establish that a profitable edge exists. Gaps, costs and correlated holdings can create losses beyond a chosen assumption.

On TradeHQ, you can practise risk-management ideas with $100,000 in virtual cash. Experiment with different position sizes, exit rules, and reward-to-risk assumptions, then review how each choice changes drawdown and variability over a larger sample of trades. The aim is to build a repeatable process, not to discover a guaranteed formula.

Position Sizing With a Predefined Risk Limit

Position sizing determines how much of your portfolio you expose to a single trade. Percentage-based limits such as 1% or 2% are common educational examples, but they are not universal prescriptions. On a $100,000 practice account, a 1% risk budget would be $1,000 and a 2% budget would be $2,000.

For a hypothetical $100,000 account, a chosen 1% worksheet loss budget is $1,000. An entry at $100 and an assumed exit at $95 create a $5 price loss per share before costs. Dividing $1,000 by $5 gives 200 shares and a $20,000 entry notional, but that excludes fees. TradeHQ's 0.1% buy and sell fees add $20 at entry and $19 at that exit, making the total loss $1,039. To include those fees in the same assumed $1,000 budget, divide by $5 + $0.10 + $0.095 = $5.195 per share: rounding down to 192 whole shares gives a $997.44 loss at exactly $95. This remains a worksheet assumption, not a guaranteed maximum loss: a gap or different fill can exceed it, and TradeHQ does not execute an automatic stop.

In a fixed-loss hypothetical model, smaller fractional losses reduce the cumulative decline relative to larger losses. Actual outcomes can exceed assumptions, particularly where fills, fees or simultaneous exposures differ. Use the simulator to compare several fixed-risk assumptions and record the resulting drawdowns rather than treating any single percentage as a magic number.

Stop-Losses and Risk-Reward Ratios

A stop order uses a trigger price, while its eventual fill depends on the order type and market conditions. Gaps or limited liquidity can produce a worse fill than the planned price. A journal exit assumption is useful for arithmetic but does not establish an exact maximum loss.

Reward-to-risk compares an assumed gain with an assumed loss. With fixed realized 3R wins and 1R losses, a 25% win rate gives 0.25×3−0.75×1=0R gross expectancy before costs. A planned target need not be achieved, and fees can make even that break-even example negative.

Compare position sizes and hypothetical exit rules in a practice journal, using the same observation period and stated cost assumptions. TradeHQ executes market orders and does not place automatic stop orders. Review drawdown, realized gains and losses, sample size and assumptions without treating any ratio as a guarantee.

Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Price Control and Execution Uncertainty
5 min read
Beginner Guide
Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Price Control and Execution Uncertainty

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: market, limit and stop order definitions and execution/price uncertainty were compared with the SEC Investor.gov Types of Orders page. Hypothetical BTC prices are illustrative, not a verified market quotation.

Compare market and limit order mechanics, fill uncertainty and the situations each order type is designed for. TradeHQ only simulates market orders.

What Is a Market Order?

A market order seeks execution at available prices rather than specifying a limit price. Execution and the final price depend on available liquidity, trading halts and other conditions. The displayed quote is not a guaranteed fill, particularly when prices move quickly.

Market orders prioritize seeking execution over a specified price limit. That trade-off can involve substantial uncertainty in the eventual fill. Compare hypothetical outcomes under different liquidity and gap assumptions rather than prescribe one order type for every urgent situation.

Slippage is the difference between an expected price and the actual fill. Its size varies with order size, liquidity and timing; it is not always pennies in a named asset. TradeHQ uses simplified practice market fills and does not reproduce every exchange execution condition.

What Is a Limit Order?

A limit order specifies the highest acceptable price for a buy or the lowest acceptable price for a sale; an execution may occur at a better price. A buy limit order executes only at your specified price or lower; a sell limit order executes only at your specified price or higher. Unlike market orders, limit orders give you price control but don't guarantee execution.

In a hypothetical example, suppose Bitcoin is quoted at $68,000 while a buy limit is set at $65,000. If the market reaches that level, the order becomes eligible to fill, subject to available liquidity and order priority. A limit instruction can also be cancelled or expire before the quoted price reaches its boundary; its lifetime depends on the specified conditions.

Limit orders can be useful when price control matters more than immediate execution. They are commonly used for planned entries and exits, but the trade-off is that the order may not fill at all, or may fill only partially, if there is not enough matching liquidity.

When to Use Each Order Type

A market order and a limit order make different trade-offs between seeking execution and controlling price. For a learning exercise, compare possible fills during a liquid session, a wide spread and a price gap. Neither urgency nor a familiar ticker guarantees a small execution cost.

A limit order specifies a maximum buy price or minimum sell price. Price control does not guarantee any fill or a full fill, even when a chart touches the level. Compare an unfilled order with a partial fill and a completed fill in a written hypothetical example.

TradeHQ currently executes market orders only. Study limit-order mechanics conceptually with a written example; there is no pending limit-order feature to test on SOL or another asset. Simulator fills cannot establish which order type gives better actual execution.

Technical Indicators Explained: RSI, MACD and Moving Averages
7 min read
Beginner Guide
Technical Indicators Explained: RSI, MACD and Moving Averages

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. Source check: 2026-10-18. RSI, MACD and moving-average definitions compared with the linked Fidelity guides; no predictive-performance or professional review claimed.

RSI, MACD and moving averages describe selected price observations. Learn their calculations, conventional interpretations and limits, then compare hypothetical examples without treating a signal as a trade recommendation.

Moving Averages: The Foundation of Trend Analysis

Moving averages smooth a selected price series rather than establish a hidden or future trend. Two commonly used calculations are the simple moving average (SMA), which weights observations in its window equally, and the exponential moving average (EMA), which gives greater weight to recent observations.

A 50-period average crossing above a 200-period average is called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. The period might mean days or another chart interval. These lagging observations describe the selected series and do not establish that a rally or decline will follow.

Shorter averages such as a 9-period or 21-period EMA react differently from longer averages. A price above an average describes its position relative to that calculation, not a guaranteed trend. TradeHQ chart controls include moving-average and volume overlays; indicator examples should match the actual chart features.

RSI: Measuring Momentum and Overbought/Oversold Conditions

Standard RSI, introduced by J. Welles Wilder, expresses the relationship between smoothed gains and losses on a 0–100 scale. Fourteen periods is a common default; the conventional thresholds are descriptive labels rather than evidence of misvaluation or future direction.

Readings above 70 or below 30 are conventional RSI descriptions rather than instructions to sell or buy. An extreme reading can persist. Divergence means price and oscillator observations differ; it does not prove a reversal or make one signal universally most reliable.

Compare hypothetical RSI settings and record what each describes before looking at later prices. A pullback to 40–50 or a bounce to 50–60 is not a universal entry rule. TradeHQ's simplified RSI-style practice value should not be mistaken for a standard RSI calculation on historical provider closes.

MACD: Combining Trend and Momentum Signals

The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) is a versatile indicator that shows the relationship between two exponential moving averages — typically the 12-period and 26-period EMAs. The MACD line is the difference between these two EMAs, and the signal line is a 9-period EMA of the MACD line. The histogram shows the gap between them.

A positive histogram means the MACD line is above its signal line; a negative histogram means it is below. Those relationships are often called bullish and bearish respectively, but describe the selected calculations rather than the next price move. Crossovers can reverse in both trending and sideways samples; performance depends on the rules, period, costs and comparison used.

Combining indicators creates another hypothesis to evaluate, rather than guaranteeing the best results. Define each calculation, interval and decision rule, then compare against a simple baseline with the same costs and sample. TradeHQ does not provide a MACD chart overlay; journal examples are conceptual.

SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON

Bitcoin vs Ethereum

Bitcoin and Ethereum are digital networks with different transaction and application designs. Compare their supply rules, uses and costs without treating either token as a savings plan or predicting its price.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Digital network asset
Bitcoin (BTC)
Practise BTC
Smart-contract platform
Ethereum (ETH)
Practise ETH
Key differences
Supply: compare Bitcoin issuance rules with Ethereum issuance and fee burning; Ethereum supply changes with network conditions.
Staking: Ethereum rewards, fees, withdrawal arrangements and risks vary; TradeHQ does not model staking returns.
Use case: compare settlement and programmability using each network’s current documentation.
Volatility: compare percentage changes over the same stated sample rather than use a fixed ETH/BTC volatility multiple.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: contrast Bitcoin supply rules and settlement design with Ethereum execution, issuance and staking mechanics. Neither profile establishes the better investment, an assured hedge or future upside.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Bitcoin and Ethereum

Bitcoin transactions transfer value under rules verified by network participants. Ethereum also supports applications through smart contracts. Those mechanisms raise different research questions: how transactions are validated, what users pay to transact, how protocol changes are adopted and how application execution works. Neither design guarantees demand for its token. Use the network documentation to distinguish technical rules from a claim about savings, purchasing power or future market price.

For a practice comparison, measure BTC and ETH returns over the same observation period. Correlation depends on that sample and can change; two token names do not by themselves establish independent exposures. Record the market-data source, interval and method before interpreting a relationship. Network activity, fees and issuance are additional variables to investigate rather than guaranteed leading indicators. A BTC/ETH split changes weights but does not prove diversification or prescribe a suitable total crypto allocation.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Treating two token names as proof of diversification. Measure correlation over a stated sample and compare combined exposure under different price shocks.
Assuming staking rewards are a guaranteed return. Withdrawal arrangements, validator penalties, service-provider costs and smart-contract risks vary with the method; token-price losses are separate.
Treating a lower unit price as proof of cheaper valuation. Units, circulating supply, issuance and the rights associated with an asset are different measures.
How to compare a practice worksheet

Create separate BTC and ETH columns for transaction validation, network fees, supply changes and custody assumptions. Cite a dated network source for each fact. In a second table, apply the same hypothetical percentage rise and fall to equal starting values, including practice fees. Keep that arithmetic separate from staking income, which TradeHQ does not pay, and from any claim that two tokens provide independent exposures. Add a row distinguishing the simulator transaction fee from a network transaction charge: the former changes virtual cash, while the latter belongs to an external network example. Check whether a quoted network cost uses native units or dollars before comparing it with another network's fee.

Equal dollar values do not establish equal risk. Record unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Provider observations and generated history are different; simulated portfolio metrics do not establish real-account drawdowns or suitability.

Sources for your research

Check the source date, reporting period and product definitions. These references explain structures and research inputs; they do not validate a price forecast.

Bitcoin vs Ethereum

Bitcoin and Ethereum are digital networks with different transaction and application designs. Compare their supply rules, uses and costs without treating either token as a savings plan or predicting its price.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Digital network asset
Bitcoin (BTC)
Practise BTC
Smart-contract platform
Ethereum (ETH)
Practise ETH
Key differences
Supply: compare Bitcoin issuance rules with Ethereum issuance and fee burning; Ethereum supply changes with network conditions.
Staking: Ethereum rewards, fees, withdrawal arrangements and risks vary; TradeHQ does not model staking returns.
Use case: compare settlement and programmability using each network’s current documentation.
Volatility: compare percentage changes over the same stated sample rather than use a fixed ETH/BTC volatility multiple.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: contrast Bitcoin supply rules and settlement design with Ethereum execution, issuance and staking mechanics. Neither profile establishes the better investment, an assured hedge or future upside.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Bitcoin and Ethereum

Bitcoin transactions transfer value under rules verified by network participants. Ethereum also supports applications through smart contracts. Those mechanisms raise different research questions: how transactions are validated, what users pay to transact, how protocol changes are adopted and how application execution works. Neither design guarantees demand for its token. Use the network documentation to distinguish technical rules from a claim about savings, purchasing power or future market price.

For a practice comparison, measure BTC and ETH returns over the same observation period. Correlation depends on that sample and can change; two token names do not by themselves establish independent exposures. Record the market-data source, interval and method before interpreting a relationship. Network activity, fees and issuance are additional variables to investigate rather than guaranteed leading indicators. A BTC/ETH split changes weights but does not prove diversification or prescribe a suitable total crypto allocation.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Treating two token names as proof of diversification. Measure correlation over a stated sample and compare combined exposure under different price shocks.
Assuming staking rewards are a guaranteed return. Withdrawal arrangements, validator penalties, service-provider costs and smart-contract risks vary with the method; token-price losses are separate.
Treating a lower unit price as proof of cheaper valuation. Units, circulating supply, issuance and the rights associated with an asset are different measures.
How to compare a practice worksheet

Create separate BTC and ETH columns for transaction validation, network fees, supply changes and custody assumptions. Cite a dated network source for each fact. In a second table, apply the same hypothetical percentage rise and fall to equal starting values, including practice fees. Keep that arithmetic separate from staking income, which TradeHQ does not pay, and from any claim that two tokens provide independent exposures. Add a row distinguishing the simulator transaction fee from a network transaction charge: the former changes virtual cash, while the latter belongs to an external network example. Check whether a quoted network cost uses native units or dollars before comparing it with another network's fee.

Equal dollar values do not establish equal risk. Record unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Provider observations and generated history are different; simulated portfolio metrics do not establish real-account drawdowns or suitability.

Check the source date, reporting period and product definitions. These references explain structures and research inputs; they do not validate a price forecast.

SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON

Tesla vs Nvidia

Tesla reports automotive and energy businesses; NVIDIA sells compute products and supporting software. Compare their business models and current filings rather than treating an AI narrative or a historical beta estimate as a permanent risk label.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

EV + energy + AI
Tesla (TSLA)
Practise TSLA
Compute products + software
Nvidia (NVDA)
Practise NVDA
Key differences
Business mix: compare automotive and energy reporting with compute products and supporting software.
Margins: use comparable periods and segment definitions from current company filings rather than fixed percentages.
Risk: compare demand, spending, competition and execution assumptions with alternative outcomes.
Beta: a beta estimate depends on the benchmark, interval and period; it is not a permanent risk score.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: contrast Tesla automotive and energy assumptions with NVIDIA compute demand and customer concentration. Neither business narrative establishes a superior investment or predictable price response.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Tesla and Nvidia

NVIDIA reporting separates compute and networking from graphics and discusses customer concentration. Tesla reporting separates automotive from energy generation and storage. Those categories suggest different questions: how customers fund compute capacity, how consumers and businesses buy vehicles, and how energy demand affects storage orders. Use current filings to measure those contributions instead of assuming a budget change produces an immediate margin or price response.

A useful reporting worksheet separates revenue, margin, capital spending and forward-looking statements. Record how each company defines its segments and whether a margin excludes particular items before comparing numbers. An earnings headline does not reveal all those inputs or establish how the share price will react. Compare reported results with clearly stated prior assumptions; avoid describing a valuation multiple or a market reaction without its date and source.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Treating both companies as one AI exposure. Compare business mix, customer demand and shared market factors rather than assuming their drivers are unrelated.
Treating a beta estimate or a familiar ticker as a guaranteed risk classification. Compare the same benchmark and sample, and consider hypothetical price shocks without prescribing leverage or a fixed drawdown.
Treating a headline earnings beat as a price forecast. Guidance, margins, expectations and wider market conditions can all matter; a positive result does not guarantee a gain.
How to compare a practice worksheet

Choose matching reporting periods from Tesla and NVIDIA. Record each company's segment revenue, the definition of a selected margin and one disclosed demand risk, with page references. Write one alternative outcome for each assumption. Keep delivery counts and compute revenue in their own units; neither is a directly comparable volume measure or a simulated earnings-trading signal. Identify whether each selected figure comes from a quarterly report, annual report or presentation. A quarter and a fiscal year cannot be compared as if they cover the same duration. Preserve the original units and any stated exclusions so that another reader can reconstruct the comparison.

Equal dollar values do not establish equal risk. Record unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Provider observations and generated history are different; simulated portfolio metrics do not establish real-account drawdowns or suitability.

Check the source date, reporting period and product definitions. These references explain structures and research inputs; they do not validate a price forecast.

SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON

Bitcoin vs Gold (GLD fund)

Gold and Bitcoin have different ownership, custody and market arrangements. A gold fund also differs from physical gold. Compare specified exposures over matching dates; neither a long history nor a digital supply rule guarantees a hedge.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Digital network asset
Bitcoin (BTC)
Practise BTC
Gold fund exposure
Gold (GLD fund) (GLD)
Practise GLD
Key differences
Volatility: compare a specified gold exposure and BTC over the same period and calculation method.
Correlation: a relationship with equities depends on the period examined and is not a permanent hedge.
Costs: physical custody, fund expenses and crypto key-management arrangements are different and require product-specific checks.
Access: trading hours and settlement depend on the instrument, venue and provider; a gold fund is not physical gold.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: contrast physical gold exposure, costs and custody with Bitcoin network and custody risks. Neither is assured currency-crisis insurance or a guarantee of asymmetric upside.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Bitcoin and Gold (GLD fund)

Gold exposure can mean physical holdings, an exchange-traded fund or a derivative, each with different ownership, custody and cost arrangements. Gold has industrial and reserve uses, but a historical role does not guarantee preservation of purchasing power or gains during market stress. Bitcoin uses a digital network with distinct supply and settlement rules. A comparison should identify the exact exposures and the observation period before describing volatility, demand or correlations; the length of a narrative is not evidence of a reliable hedge.

In a hypothetical stress exercise, compare several possible price changes for gold and Bitcoin rather than assume one rises whenever stocks fall. Use equal starting values and record the resulting portfolio contribution, costs and custody assumptions. A recent favourable response does not establish a permanent safe-haven relationship. Different custody methods introduce different operational risks, and neither a price chart nor a simulated return certifies real-money suitability. TradeHQ can illustrate price and portfolio arithmetic without reproducing physical delivery or key custody.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Assuming equal dollar positions have equal risk. Compare variability and portfolio contributions under stated data and assumptions; no relative position size is prescribed.
Calling an asset an inflation hedge from one favorable period. Define the inflation measure, dates and specific exposure before evaluating a relationship; it may change in another sample.
Treating a gold fund as physical delivery. Fund expenses, physical storage and Bitcoin custody involve different arrangements and product-specific costs.
How to compare a practice worksheet

Label the gold column GLD fund exposure, not a bar in a vault. Read the fund's expense and custody descriptions alongside Bitcoin's transaction and wallet documentation. Compare equal hypothetical starting values under both rising and falling price scenarios, with a separate column for costs excluded by the simulator. Do not label either result an inflation hedge without matching dated market and inflation data.

Equal dollar values do not establish equal risk. Record unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Provider observations and generated history are different; simulated portfolio metrics do not establish real-account drawdowns or suitability.

Sources for your research

Check the source date, reporting period and product definitions. These references explain structures and research inputs; they do not validate a price forecast.

SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON

Apple vs Microsoft

Apple and Microsoft are both large technology companies, but their business mixes differ. Apple combines consumer hardware with services and capital returns, while Microsoft combines enterprise software, cloud infrastructure and AI-related products. A useful comparison starts with those business models rather than a short-term price forecast.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Consumer hardware + services
Apple (AAPL)
Practise AAPL
Enterprise software + cloud
Microsoft (MSFT)
Practise MSFT
Key differences
Revenue mix: compare Apple's hardware and services contribution with Microsoft's productivity, cloud and other enterprise businesses.
AI exposure: compare how each company describes AI-related products, infrastructure spending and monetisation in its current filings.
Capital return: both companies return cash to shareholders; check current dividends, repurchases and share-count changes in their latest reports.
Regulation: both operate under changing competition, platform, privacy and technology rules, so use current filings rather than a permanent regulatory label.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: examine Apple's hardware, services and capital-return model alongside Microsoft's enterprise software, cloud and AI-infrastructure model. Neither profile is automatically the better investment; the relevant risks and valuation assumptions differ.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Apple and Microsoft

Apple's economics combine device sales with recurring services tied to its installed base. When analysing the business, useful questions include how hardware demand changes, how services contribute to revenue and margins, and how dividends or share repurchases affect per-share results. Those figures should be taken from the latest Apple filings because they change over time.

Microsoft's economics are heavily connected to enterprise software, subscriptions and cloud infrastructure. Its current reporting also discusses substantial investment in capacity for cloud and AI workloads. When comparing it with Apple, separate revenue growth from the cost of supporting that growth and use the latest Microsoft filings for current rates, spending and segment definitions. Use comparable reporting periods when comparing growth, margins and cash returns.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Treating a mega-cap company as low risk simply because it is large. Large companies can still experience substantial drawdowns and business-model changes.
Comparing headline per-share metrics without checking share-count changes, capital spending and cash returns. Those factors can alter what per-share growth means.
Assuming an index position gives the same exposure for every investor. If you are comparing a single stock with an index fund, check the fund's current holdings and weights first.
How to compare a practice worksheet

Use Apple and Microsoft filings from comparable reporting periods. Record hardware/services and enterprise/cloud segment definitions, capital spending and share-count changes. Mark any metric that cannot be compared directly. Explain how a share-count change could affect a per-share measure without changing the total business result; do not convert that explanation into a share-price prediction.

Equal dollar values do not establish equal risk. Record unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Provider observations and generated history are different; simulated portfolio metrics do not establish real-account drawdowns or suitability.

mainText:
SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON

Ethereum vs Solana

Ethereum and Solana use different designs for processing transactions and supporting applications. Compare current network documentation, transaction definitions and fee measurements rather than assigning permanent leadership or token-price upside.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

L1 + L2 ecosystem
Ethereum (ETH)
Practise ETH
Integrated execution network
Solana (SOL)
Practise SOL
Key differences
Throughput: define transaction type, observation period and inclusion of votes or rollup activity before comparing counts.
Fees: actual fees vary with transaction type and network conditions; no fixed cost range is established here.
Reliability: compare documented incidents and their dates rather than claim that a network has never halted.
Staking: rewards, issuance, fees and operational risks differ; advertised yield is not a guaranteed real return.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: contrast network design, execution, reliability and supply assumptions using current Ethereum and Solana documentation. Throughput or a fee comparison does not establish token-price upside.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Ethereum and Solana

A network comparison should identify where execution happens and how results are verified. Ethereum's scaling documentation discusses layer-2 rollups with different security models; a mainnet transaction and a rollup transaction should not be counted interchangeably. Solana's documentation describes its own account and transaction model. Compare a specific operation, confirmation criterion and observation window before quoting throughput or fees. Network requirements, validator participation and reliability need dated evidence rather than permanent rankings.

Network activity and token returns are different measures. A comparison can examine where fees are charged, how supply changes and which security assumptions apply without presuming that greater activity raises price. Staking rewards are denominated in the token and can be affected by costs, issuance, protocol rules and market-price losses. Comparing nominal reward percentages alone does not establish an inflation-adjusted investment return. Document the source and period and separate the network’s design from a forecast of its token’s value.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Choosing on transactions per second alone. A benchmark describes its test conditions. Observed throughput, congestion and reliability must be compared using consistent definitions.
Reading a token reward percentage as a cash return. State the period, token-price change, fees, penalties and supply assumptions; subtracting issuance alone does not calculate an investor's return.
Predicting a token-price response from an outage. Record the incident's date, duration and affected services separately from any claim about adoption or price.
How to compare a practice worksheet

Choose the same type of application operation on Ethereum and Solana. Record whether Ethereum activity is on mainnet or a named layer 2, what each transaction count includes, how confirmation is defined and when fees were measured. Put reliability incidents in a separate dated log. Leave token-price forecasts out of the table: neither a faster operation nor a lower fee establishes investment performance.

Equal dollar values do not establish equal risk. Record unfavorable as well as favorable cases. Provider observations and generated history are different; simulated portfolio metrics do not establish real-account drawdowns or suitability.

Software: compare current product documentation and compatibility rather than presume permanent developer lock-in.
Margins: use current company filings with matching periods and segment definitions.
Valuation: calculate a stated valuation measure from dated inputs; it is not a permanent premium.
Demand: compare reported compute spending and competing outcomes; share gains do not guarantee a stock re-rating.
What the comparison shows

Practice comparison: examine product mix, software support, customer demand and reported costs. Neither incumbency nor a challenger narrative establishes compounding dominance or greater share-price upside.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

What actually separates Nvidia and AMD

Hardware and software should be examined together. For a stated workload, check supported models, libraries, numerical precision, memory and deployment requirements in each vendor's documentation. Then separate those compatibility findings from company-level revenue, costs and customer risks in the filings. A benchmark result describes its test setup; it does not establish purchasing decisions, a permanent software advantage or future market share. Version and date the comparison because supported products and tools change.

A market-share hypothesis and a stock-price response are different propositions. Compare what was known before an announcement with alternative expectations and reported results. Customer spending, supply, competition, software compatibility and costs can affect both companies, but that does not establish a predictable asymmetric reaction. Prices can reflect varying expectations and other market factors; a positive business development need not produce a gain. Use matched reporting periods and dated inputs when comparing valuation or profitability.

Common mistakes with this comparison
Treating one benchmark as proof of market share. Check the workload, software version, availability and disclosed customer arrangements separately.
Calling two compute stocks a guaranteed hedge. Shared demand factors do not establish equal or opposite price responses; TradeHQ does not open short positions.

Digital network asset vs Smart-contract platform
Bitcoin vs Ethereum

Bitcoin and Ethereum are digital networks with different transaction and application designs. Compare their supply rules, uses and costs without treating either token as a savings plan or predicting its price.

EV + energy + AI vs Compute products + software
Tesla vs Nvidia

Tesla reports automotive and energy businesses; NVIDIA sells compute products and supporting software. Compare their business models and current filings rather than treating an AI narrative or a historical beta estimate as a permanent risk label.

Digital network asset vs Gold fund exposure
Bitcoin vs Gold (GLD fund)

Gold and Bitcoin have different ownership, custody and market arrangements. A gold fund also differs from physical gold. Compare specified exposures over matching dates; neither a long history nor a digital supply rule guarantees a hedge.

Consumer hardware + services vs Enterprise software + cloud
Apple vs Microsoft

Apple and Microsoft are both large technology companies, but their business mixes differ. Apple combines consumer hardware with services and capital returns, while Microsoft combines enterprise software, cloud infrastructure and AI-related products. A useful comparison starts with those business models rather than a short-term price forecast.

Ethereum vs Solana

Ethereum and Solana use different designs for processing transactions and supporting applications. Compare current network documentation, transaction definitions and fee measurements rather than assigning permanent leadership or token-price upside.

Equities and crypto represent very different kinds of exposure: equities are ownership claims on businesses, while crypto assets depend on network use, market structure and investor demand. This comparison focuses on those structural differences rather than prescribing an allocation.

Nvidia vs AMD

mainText:
CRYPTO GUIDE

Learn Bitcoin — Virtual Practice

Bitcoin is a digital asset with a protocol-defined issuance schedule. Its market price is separate from that schedule and can change without a protocol change.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Practise BTC now
QUICK ANSWER
What does the Bitcoin virtual practice guide explain?

Bitcoin is a digital asset with a protocol-defined issuance schedule. Its market price is separate from that schedule and can change without a protocol change. The worksheet compares fictional quantities, prices and costs; no transaction is required to study it. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Step-by-step
1
Compare the coin’s percentage change with whole-account return using cash and holding values.
2
Visit /trade/btc and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance.
3
Using a hypothetical BTC holding of 0.05 units at $50,000 per unit, calculate $2,500 of virtual exposure and a $2.50 entry fee at the simulator's 0.1% rate; then compare with the displayed practice quote.
4
Record the dated BTC quote and an alternative 10% down-price case. For the same 0.05 BTC, that implies a $250 gross holding loss before fees, not a 10% loss of the whole $100,000 account.
5
Create a second BTC price scenario with the same unit count so gross holding return and total-account return can be compared.
Beginner tip

Begin with the difference between coin return and account return. A hypothetical 10% BTC rise applied to a $10,000 holding adds $1,000 before costs, while an otherwise cash-only $100,000 account rises only 1%. The same headline percentage can therefore describe a much larger asset move than portfolio move.

Risk warning

BTC price risk and quote-data risk are distinct. A correctly identified asset can still have an older provider observation; a recent page fetch does not make that observation current. A small BTC weight can limit its contribution to one assumed account move, but it cannot prevent the holding from losing value. Real execution is not reproduced by a paper mark.

Student perspective

A short BTC study session can focus on one unit conversion: coin quantity × dollars per coin. Keep virtual accounting separate from questions about real wallets, local access or funding. The practice account holds no real coins and makes no on-chain transfer; current eligibility and tax questions belong to official local information.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Factors to distinguish when studying Bitcoin
Compare the protocol supply schedule, exchange trading activity and news claims as separate sources of information. A halving event does not by itself determine the direction or timing of a price change.
Compare a dated primary description of Bitcoin with the practice chart. A simulated movement is not evidence that a particular news item changed the real market price.
Worked hypothetical practice example

Use a hypothetical $100,000 account with $90,000 cash and a $10,000 BTC holding before fees. A selected 10% BTC rise takes the holding to $11,000 and total value to $101,000, before excluded costs. The asset return is 10%; account return is 1%. The current holding weight is $11,000 ÷ $101,000 = about 10.89%, not 11% of the original balance. If the $10,000 purchase incurred the simulator’s 0.1% fee, cash would instead be $89,990 and total marked equity $100,990. These inputs teach accounting rather than recommend exposure.

Market sessions and observation limitations

Compare BTC’s provider observation timestamp with the chart’s source label. A periodically refreshed reference can differ from a venue’s last trade or a different-minute quote without proving either is fraudulent. Save the observation time used in your worksheet so that a later account change can be reconstructed. Opening the page is not an exchange fill.

Common mistakes specific to Bitcoin
Reporting the BTC return as the entire account return despite a large cash balance.
Calculating new allocation with the original account denominator.
Calling an aggregate provider mark a reserved exchange fill.
Ignoring both buy and sell fees in the result.
How to review the trade afterwards

Write the position’s percentage move, dollar change and whole-account return on separate lines. Recompute allocation using the new total. Then reconcile fees and inspect observation age. This review can help distinguish an asset's movement from the account return and preserve unfavorable as well as favorable cases.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

title: Learn Ethereum — Virtual Practice Guide | TradeHQ
mainText:
CRYPTO GUIDE

Learn Ethereum — Virtual Practice

Ethereum is a network for running applications and smart contracts; ether, or ETH, is its native currency. People use ETH to pay network fees, transfer value and participate in staking. Trading ETH means exchanging that currency at a market price. TradeHQ lets you practise the price and quantity calculations with virtual funds; it does not send coins to a wallet or stake them.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Practise ETH now
QUICK ANSWER
What does the Ethereum virtual practice guide explain?

Ethereum is a network for running applications and smart contracts; ether, or ETH, is its native currency. People use ETH to pay network fees, transfer value and participate in staking. Trading ETH means exchanging that currency at a market price. TradeHQ lets you practise the price and quantity calculations with virtual funds; it does not send coins to a wallet or stake them. The worksheet compares fictional quantities, prices and costs; no transaction is required to study it. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Step-by-step
1
Identify ether (ETH) as Ethereum’s native currency. Read the ETH/USD quote, its timestamp and the source before considering a hypothetical order; an indicative price is not a guaranteed execution price.
2
Visit /trade/eth and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance.
3
Use 0.5 ETH at an illustrative $3,200 quote to calculate $1,600 of virtual exposure and a $1.60 simulator entry fee. That is separate from real blockchain gas charges, which TradeHQ does not execute.
4
Record a second hypothetical ETH price and calculate the change for the same 0.5 ETH. Check the page's quote timestamp; a price screenshot cannot reveal the gas or exchange costs of a real transfer.
5
For the fictional example, review changes in ETH units, cash and simulator fees. Keep real Ethereum network gas and staking separate: TradeHQ neither transfers nor stakes coins.
Beginner tip

Separate the network from the currency: Ethereum is the system, while ETH is the unit whose price you see. A lower price per coin than BTC does not by itself mean ETH is cheaper in valuation terms.

Risk warning

Network fees, staking mechanics and ETH market-price exposure are different risks and activities. TradeHQ illustrates only the supported virtual spot accounting; it does not stake ETH, transfer coins or pay staking rewards. A correct network explanation cannot establish which direction the market price will move. Include the actual simulator fees when assessing a paper outcome.

Student perspective

Use this guide to learn the difference between Ethereum as a network and ETH as a unit. A classroom example can compare exchange fees and hypothetical network charges without funding a wallet. Local real-asset access, eligibility and taxes require current official sources; a simulator lesson is not permission to transact.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Factors to distinguish when studying Ethereum
Network use and ETH price measure different things. Gas is the unit used to measure transaction work; the network fee is paid in ETH. A busy network can change fees without producing a matching percentage change in the exchange price.
Staking helps secure Ethereum, while layer-two networks handle activity with a different fee structure. These concepts explain how the network works; a TradeHQ price chart does not measure staking rewards, network demand or the effect of a particular headline.
Worked hypothetical practice example

For a hypothetical buy of 2 ETH at $2,500 per ETH, notional is $5,000 and the simulator’s 0.1% purchase fee is $5. The cash debit is $5,005. If the later quote is $2,400, the marked holding is $4,800, giving a $200 price loss and $205 equity reduction after the purchase fee. A sale at that quote would add a $4.80 exit fee. A separately quoted blockchain gas fee is not a simulator cost: this paper buy did not create a network transaction or send ETH to a wallet.

Market sessions and observation limitations

A provider can aggregate ETH market observations while a blockchain explorer describes network activity. Match the question to the source: exchange-price timestamps for paper valuation, network records for transaction mechanics. Do not use a synthetic practice candle as evidence that a gas-fee change caused a real price reaction.

Common mistakes specific to Ethereum
Adding a real blockchain gas charge to a paper buy that sent no coins.
Describing virtual ETH as staked funds earning rewards.
Comparing whole-coin prices as if they establish relative business valuation.
Mixing dollar loss with loss per ETH unit.
How to review the trade afterwards

After the exercise, reconcile ETH units, notional cost, simulator fee and cash separately. If the quote moves $100 per ETH and you own 2 ETH, the gross marked change is $200. A gas-charge discussion belongs in a separate network worksheet. Check that neither staking income nor a wallet transfer was invented in the virtual ledger.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Network concepts: Ethereum.org on ether and Ethereum.org on gas and fees.

QUICK ANSWER
What does the Tesla virtual practice guide explain?

Tesla is a listed company. A simulated TSLA holding represents a stock-price exercise and does not provide options exposure, voting rights or actual share ownership. Company results and delivery reports are different information sets. The worksheet compares fictional quantities, prices and costs; no transaction is required to study it. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Step-by-step
1
Write the report metric you intend to investigate and a separate hypothetical gap case before viewing the outcome.
2
Visit /trade/tsla and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance.
3
For a hypothetical four-share TSLA market order at $200 per share, calculate $800 of exposure plus the $0.80 simulator entry fee. Label the chosen price illustrative, not a current Tesla quote.
4
Compare a $200 virtual entry with an assumed $180 next-session opening price. Four shares would show an $80 gross loss before costs; an intended exit is not a guaranteed fill across an overnight gap.
5
Record an alternative next-session opening price in the worksheet to show how an overnight gap can differ from an intended exit.
Beginner tip

Read deliveries, revenue and profit margins as separate measurements. A hypothetical rise in units delivered does not imply the same rise in revenue, because prices and product mix can change. A stock-price reaction also depends on expectations that a short headline may omit.

Risk warning

An event-sensitive stock worksheet should distinguish a chosen exit threshold from the next observed price. A gap can cross the threshold, and a journal note is not an automated order. Delivery growth alone cannot validate a price target. The simulator does not reproduce real opening-auction fills, shareholder rights or options exposure.

Student perspective

A TSLA study task can separate an observable report metric from an interpretation: “deliveries rose” is different from “profit must rise” or “the stock must rally.” Use a dated primary company record when investigating those claims. Record the $200 planned threshold loss and $400 stressed price loss as different assumptions, then include fees when reviewing net equity.

Attach a date and reporting period to any delivery or earnings evidence. Then note whether the chart represents provider history or synthetic practice candles. Treating delivery volume as interchangeable with revenue or profit.
Calling a journal exit threshold an executed stop order.
Deleting a gap case because it exceeded the chosen worksheet loss.
Inventing a report-based reason after seeing the stock movement.

Compare the original thesis with the information actually available before the exercise. Did you mean delivery volume, revenue or margins? Reconstruct shares, assumed entry, observed mark and fees. STOCK GUIDE

Learn Nvidia — Virtual Practice

Nvidia supplies computing products and services. Its share price and its operating business are different objects: a change in sales does not translate mechanically into the same percentage stock return.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Practise NVDA now
QUICK ANSWER
What does the Nvidia virtual practice guide explain?

Nvidia supplies computing products and services. Its share price and its operating business are different objects: a change in sales does not translate mechanically into the same percentage stock return. The worksheet compares fictional quantities, prices and costs; no transaction is required to study it. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Step-by-step
1
List direct company exposure and any assumed fund overlap before computing the combined account weight.
2
Visit /trade/nvda and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance.
3
Using five hypothetical NVDA shares at $120 each, calculate a $600 virtual position and $0.60 simulated entry fee. Do not treat the worksheet price as a live quotation.
4
Record any NVDA weight already held inside a chosen ETF using that fund's dated holdings report, then combine direct and indirect exposure before interpreting an illustrative price change.
5
Compare direct NVIDIA shares with a hypothetical dated ETF allocation to identify potential overlap before interpreting a percentage change.
Beginner tip

Separate company operating measures from the share-price return. A hypothetical 20% sales increase and a 5% stock decline can coexist when expectations, costs or guidance differ. The price observation alone does not tell you which explanation is correct.

Risk warning

Direct NVDA shares can overlap a technology or broad-market fund you also hold. Row count is therefore an incomplete diversification measure. Inspect actual fund weights and their dates before computing look-through exposure. Company sales growth and diversification labels do not guarantee protection from losses or a positive share-price response.

Student perspective

A useful NVDA learning task can be done without a directional bet: compare the meaning of sales, earnings and market capitalization, then calculate a small hypothetical holding. Real share access and local obligations are separate questions. A virtual price gain does not verify an ability to assess a company’s fair value.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Factors to distinguish when studying Nvidia
Company results, customer spending statements, supply constraints and export rules can provide business context. Verify any current figures from dated primary reports; none of these topics establishes that a trend-following strategy will outperform.
Compare a dated primary description of Nvidia with the practice chart. A simulated movement is not evidence that a particular news item changed the real market price.
Worked hypothetical practice example

Imagine a $10,000 worksheet with $2,000 held directly in NVDA and $8,000 in a fund. Assume, only for this exercise, that the fund has a 10% NVDA weight. The indirect exposure is $800, so combined NVDA exposure is $2,800, or 28% of total value. Counting two account rows misses this overlap. A selected 10% NVDA fall contributes $280 of loss through the two exposures using the initial exposures and assuming other holdings stay unchanged. Real fund weights need a dated holdings source; the assumed 10% is not a current portfolio fact.

Market sessions and observation limitations

Distinguish a dated financial statement, guidance and an intraday price quote. They answer different questions and update on different schedules. A synthetic chart cannot validate a claim about customer demand. In a report exercise, write what the market was expected to learn as well as what the company announced.

Common mistakes specific to Nvidia
Counting a fund and direct shares as wholly independent exposures.
Using an undated assumed fund weight as a current fact.
Assuming a sales-growth percentage dictates the stock-return percentage.
Inferring fair value from the nominal price of one share.
How to review the trade afterwards

Review both the direct holding and any assumed fund overlap. Record whether fund weights were actual dated inputs or deliberately hypothetical. Recompute the account denominator after price changes, and separate operating metrics from share-price results. The goal is a reproducible exposure explanation, not a claim that two technology labels imply diversification.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

ETF GUIDE

Learn S&P 500 ETF — Virtual Practice

SPY is an exchange-traded fund designed to track the S&P 500. An index methodology, a fund holding and a country economy are different things; broad coverage does not remove market losses or concentration.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Practise SPY now
QUICK ANSWER
What does the S&P 500 ETF virtual practice guide explain?

SPY is an exchange-traded fund designed to track the S&P 500. An index methodology, a fund holding and a country economy are different things; broad coverage does not remove market losses or concentration. The worksheet compares fictional quantities, prices and costs; no transaction is required to study it. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Step-by-step
1
Identify fund units and current account weight; label any distribution or fund-expense concepts not simulated.
2
Visit /trade/spy and read the quote and chart data-status labels; they may have different provenance.
3
For two illustrative SPY units at $500 each, calculate $1,000 of virtual fund exposure and a $1 simulated entry fee. Keep the unit price distinct from the fund's constituent-stock prices.
4
Calculate the combined account weight of this $1,000 fund exposure and any direct shares that overlap its disclosed holdings; note that distributions, expense ratios and full tracking effects are not modelled in the basic virtual order.
5
Label how the ETF's distribution and operating costs are outside the simplified practice order, and calculate exposure against total account value.
Beginner tip

An ETF unit represents fund exposure; it is not a direct account row for each constituent company. Nominal share price also differs from the dollars you hold. Twenty $50 units and two $500 units both make $1,000 positions before fees.

Risk warning

A broad fund can reduce exposure to one company while remaining exposed to market losses and overlap with direct stocks. Diversification is not immunity. Actual fund constituents and weights require dated disclosures, and a fixed index name does not establish that every constituent contributes equally to your result.

Student perspective

SPY can teach the distinction between an index, a fund and a virtual holding. A learner can inspect a dated fund description and calculate a hypothetical exposure without acquiring real units. The worksheet is not a claim about local fund eligibility, investment suitability or tax treatment.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Factors to distinguish when studying S&P 500 ETF
Fund holdings, index methodology, distributions and expenses describe the instrument. Consult current fund documents for those details. An index comparison can be a benchmark, but a short practice sample cannot prove an investing strategy is better.
Compare a dated primary description of S&P 500 ETF with the practice chart. A simulated movement is not evidence that a particular news item changed the real market price.
Worked hypothetical practice example

A hypothetical SPY worksheet holds ten units at $500, or $5,000, while the account has $95,000 cash before purchase fees. A selected 2% price decline changes the holding to $4,900: a $100 price loss, or 0.1% of the original $100,000 account. The simulator purchase fee on $5,000 is $5. If marked at the lower quote after that fee, equity would be $99,895. Fund-level holdings, distributions and expenses are separate concepts; this simple paper mark does not reproduce a complete fund accounting statement.

Market sessions and observation limitations

A recently fetched fund quote can still refer to an earlier market observation, particularly outside the relevant session. Read the source and observation time rather than calling a weekend page refresh a new trade. The simulator’s chart status also determines whether candles are provider history or synthetic practice inputs.

Common mistakes specific to S&P 500 ETF
Describing fund units as direct ownership of every index constituent.
Treating a broad-market fund as unable to lose value.
Ignoring overlap between the fund and separately held company shares.
Inventing a cash distribution that the simulator did not record.
How to review the trade afterwards

Review units, the marked price and whole-account exposure separately. Explain how the $100 holding loss becomes a much smaller account percentage because most of this worksheet is cash. Include fees and note any distribution or expense mechanics excluded from the simulator rather than silently inventing cash entries.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

CRYPTO GUIDE

Learn Solana — Virtual Practice

SOL is Solana's native token, while Solana is the network on which SOL is used for transaction fees. Learning to read a SOL price quote is not the same as transferring SOL on-chain, staking tokens or trading a derivatives contract. TradeHQ offers a virtual spot-price practice exercise only.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Practise SOL now
QUICK ANSWER
What does the Solana virtual practice guide explain?

SOL is Solana's native token, while Solana is the network on which SOL is used for transaction fees. Learning to read a SOL price quote is not the same as transferring SOL on-chain, staking tokens or trading a derivatives contract. TradeHQ offers a virtual spot-price practice exercise only. The worksheet compares fictional quantities, prices and costs; no transaction is required to study it. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Step-by-step
1
Identify the instrument before doing any arithmetic: SOL is the token, a SOL/USD quote is a price per token, and an exchange venue's quoted price may differ from a separate source. Record the quote currency, source and observation time.
2
Choose a hypothetical dollar budget and SOL unit price. Divide budget by unit price to calculate units, then add the simulator's stated 0.1% virtual order fee to estimate cash required. Use amounts solely for the worksheet, not as a recommended allocation.
3
On /trade/sol, inspect the quoted spot price and any data-status label. No order is required for this worksheet; the simulator does not support resting limit or stop orders, short positions or staking.
4
Write two different exit-price scenarios before reading a later quote. Calculate gross profit or loss as units times the change in dollars per SOL; subtract hypothetical buy and sell transaction fees separately.
5
Review what the exercise could and could not show: quote observation versus actual fill, changes in SOL value versus whole-portfolio return, and missing real-world exchange costs, spread, slippage and custody.
Beginner tip

The simulated SOL holding represents exposure to token-price changes, not ownership in Solana Labs or an entitlement to network revenue. Network transaction fees paid in SOL, token-staking mechanics and the cost of buying or selling SOL on an exchange are distinct concepts. The TradeHQ spot simulation does not perform blockchain transactions or staking.

Risk warning

SOL's token price can move rapidly in either direction. Exchange liquidity, order size, spread and execution terms affect an actual fill; network reliability and token supply information do not predict the next price. In a simulator, a displayed mark and a later virtual fill may not recreate exchange execution or custody risk. Never equate a hypothetical outcome with achievable returns.

Student perspective

This example is entirely virtual and does not require a wallet, real funds or access to an exchange. Laws and access conditions vary by jurisdiction; a financial-education worksheet is not confirmation that a venue or product is available locally.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Factors to distinguish when studying Solana
Read Solana's primary documentation to distinguish network transaction processing and fee mechanics from exchange spot trading. Usage and technology changes may matter to market participants, but they do not determine a particular SOL price or return.
Compare two dated, clearly identified price observations before calculating a percentage change. Network or ecosystem news may coincide with price movements without demonstrating that it caused them.
Worked hypothetical practice example

Hypothetical example, not live market data: suppose SOL is $125 and the practice order is 40 SOL. The gross purchase value is 40 × $125 = $5,000; a 0.1% virtual buy fee is $5. If the later assumed price is $130, gross marked value is 40 × $130 = $5,200 and the gross change is $200. A hypothetical sale at $130 with a further 0.1% simulator fee of $5.20 would make the round-trip result $189.80 before any costs not simulated. If SOL instead fell to $115, the holding would be worth $4,600: a $400 gross decline before fees. These are chosen numbers, not a forecast or a liquidity guarantee.

Market sessions and observation limitations

Digital-asset venues may operate around the clock, but 24/7 access does not mean identical liquidity at every moment. Compare source timestamp, spreads and event conditions when studying external market data. TradeHQ's chart can be sourced differently from its quote; inspect the data labels and avoid treating a chart candle as proof that a real-world market order would fill at that exact price.

Common mistakes specific to Solana
Confusing an exchange SOL price with the on-chain fee for sending a Solana transaction.
Using a marked portfolio value as if it were a guaranteed executable sale price.
Ignoring the second virtual fee when calculating a hypothetical round trip.
Assuming network usage or a technical announcement guarantees token-price appreciation.
How to review the trade afterwards

Record the hypothetical buy and sell prices, quantity, both virtual fees, source timestamps and portfolio allocation. Separate token return from total-account return and note which slippage, spread and custody costs the simulation omits. Try a lower exit-price case as well as a higher one to test the same arithmetic.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

mainText:
TRADING STRATEGY

Scalping

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. No independent professional review is claimed.

A short-horizon price and transaction-cost comparison; no fixed interval defines the concept.

Open spot-order practice
QUICK ANSWER
What is the Scalping trading strategy and does it work?

Scalping: A short-horizon price and transaction-cost comparison; no fixed interval defines the concept. No universal win rate or sufficient sample size applies. Recorded hypothetical outcomes depend on the sample design, assumptions and costs. Study context: A study of how spreads, fees and latency affect short-horizon calculations; not a suitability recommendation. Use the worksheet below to examine the example rules. TradeHQ’s separate $100,000 spot simulator does not implement every indicator or strategy. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Study context

A study of how spreads, fees and latency affect short-horizon calculations; not a suitability recommendation.

Limitations

Simplified fills and generated candles do not reproduce order-book priority, partial fills or intraday liquidity.

Hypothetical study steps
1
Choose one instrument and explicitly fictional entry, exit and cost inputs for a short-horizon worksheet.
2
State the chart interval and whether the observations are provider history or generated practice candles.
3
Calculate the effect of a worse fill and a wider spread before comparing gains and losses.
4
Record all selected cases, including unfavorable ones. TradeHQ supports manual market orders; planned stops are worksheet assumptions.
Worked example

Hypothetical one-BTC worksheet: buy at $95,120 and compare exits at $95,210 and $95,080. Before costs, these are a $90 gain and a $40 loss. At TradeHQ's 0.1% fee on each side, the entry fee is $95.12. Selling at $95,210 adds a $95.21 fee, turning the gross gain into a $100.33 net loss. Selling at $95,080 adds a $95.08 fee, making the net loss $230.20. The exit prices are assumptions, not resting stop or target orders; a real fill can differ.

Where this method comes from

Scalping describes attempts to capture small changes over short intervals. Because the intended price change is small, a spread, fee or execution delay can form a large part of the result. A two-tick cost is 20% of a ten-tick gross target, but that ratio does not establish expected profit: win frequency, adverse outcomes and all costs would also be needed.

Sample and market limitations

Liquidity and spreads vary by venue, instrument, session and event. A small spread observed in one period is not a permanent property or a reliable profit opportunity. Compare observations over stated dates rather than assign universally favorable trading hours.

Interpretation pitfalls
Comparing a gross target with a result after fees as if they were the same measure.
Treating a generated candle as evidence of an actual order-book fill.
Changing size or exit assumptions after seeing the result and combining the changed rule with the original sample.
Worked arithmetic

For the same one-BTC example, cash paid is $95,120 × 1.001 = $95,215.12. Net sale proceeds at $95,210 are $95,210 × 0.999 = $95,114.79, so the round-trip result is −$100.33. The fee-only break-even exit solves exit price × 0.999 = $95,215.12, or approximately $95,310.43 before any additional costs. A higher assumed win rate cannot make this selected $95,210 exit profitable after those fees. These are hypothetical prices, not a return forecast.

Figures are illustrative teaching examples, not projections of your results. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Realistic expectations

No universal win rate or sufficient sample size applies. Recorded hypothetical outcomes depend on the sample design, assumptions and costs.

(Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Limitations

Manual review leaves exposure between observations, and an intended exit can be crossed by a gap.

Hypothetical study steps
1

3
Compare different gap sizes and exit distances, including an unfilled or worse-than-planned exit.

Worked example

In a fictional multi-session price series, compare an initial observation with a later higher observation and a later lower observation. A price gap can cross an assumed review threshold. Neither a threshold nor a selected favorable case establishes actual execution or likely returns.

Where this method comes from

Swing trading describes positions held across sessions, often over days or weeks. The label does not determine a suitable position size or make the decision less consequential. A scheduled review can fit some learners’ routines, but holdings remain exposed between observations and suitability cannot be inferred from employment status. Overnight gaps are possible when information arrives between sessions; a worksheet threshold is not an execution guarantee.

Sample and market limitations

An apparent trend or pullback is a description of selected past data. A later continuation and a reversal are both possible. Earnings and other announcements can introduce overnight gaps; a planned exit does not guarantee a fill at that price.

Treating a round-number exit or volatility multiple as guaranteed loss protection.
Assuming favorable earnings or a company narrative determines the next opening price.
Adding to a position while reporting results as though exposure had stayed fixed.
